title: Josh Galecki - Procedurally Generating Puzzles
speaker: Josh Galecki
summary: Josh Galecki, solo developer of the nonviolent farming roguelite Moondrop, explains how to put puzzles in a repetition-driven genre by designing puzzle systems that generate solvable puzzles on demand. He distinguishes an analytic strategy (proving every configuration of a puzzle space is solvable, shown with a 2x4 Lights Out variant) from a constructive strategy (building a puzzle around a known solution, shown with a river-and-dams grid). He also covers search-based construction with a wheat maze and a failure case where the maze could become unsolvable, and how he guarded against it. He closes by recommending mathematics, especially graph theory, as a source of themed puzzle ideas.

insights.claim: Because roguelikes are built around repetition and a puzzle is trivial the second time and a chore the twentieth, roguelike puzzles must come from puzzle systems that generate new instances on demand.
insights.detail: Galecki made Moondrop, a nonviolent farming roguelike, and used puzzles instead of combat to challenge players exploring its dungeons. Puzzles also change pace in action games and deliver the 'a-ha' moment.
insights.quote: solving a puzzle once is fun. Solving it twice is trivial. And solving it for the 20th time is a chore

insights.claim: There are two strategies for guaranteeing generated puzzles are solvable: analytic (prove every configuration of the puzzle space can be solved) and constructive (build each puzzle around a known solution).
insights.detail: Galecki draws on his maths and computer science study: maths classes proved a solution exists, CS classes gave an algorithm producing one. Like the mathematician in his opening joke, the goal is just to show a solution exists.
insights.quote: the analytic shows any generated puzzle has to be solvable and the constructive is building a particular puzzle so that it has a known solution

insights.claim: Moondrop's 2x4 Lights Out lantern puzzle can start from any random configuration because move cancellation, single-switch toggle sequences and board symmetry together prove every state is solvable.
insights.detail: Toggling a switch twice cancels out regardless of moves in between; sequences exist to toggle the top-left and top-middle switches alone; symmetry extends these to all eight. So any configuration is solvable, and a minimal solution needs at most eight moves, without the designer needing to know the solutions.
insights.quote: That means that I can generate any initial configuration of on and off lanterns and I know a solution exists

insights.claim: Moondrop's river-grid puzzle is built constructively: place locked dams, place must-close and must-open toggleable dams, record target water levels at four vertices, then randomise the toggles before the player arrives.
insights.detail: Water flows down and right through a 4x4 directed graph; vertex level is the sum of incoming edges. Because the solution was built in, Galecki knows at least one exists and is fine if there are more.
insights.quote: I know that it is a solvable puzzle and there has to be because that's the way I built it

insights.claim: Moondrop's wheat maze grows by repeatedly opening a candidate tile with exactly one open neighbour and walling candidates with more, producing a loop-free branching maze that usually spans the grid.
insights.detail: The maze's tiles all look alike so players can't easily tell their location. Galecki shows open, possible and wall tiles during construction.
insights.quote: we take a possible tile that has exactly 1 open neighbor and we make it open. If it has more than one open neighbor, it becomes a wall

insights.claim: Search-based puzzle generators can fail silently, as Moondrop's maze could wall off its last tile and become unsolvable, so designers must hunt for counterexamples and add guards.
insights.detail: If the algorithm picked the wrong one of two final candidate tiles, the maze had no solution. Galecki's fix: if no open neighbour is found, carve a path toward the start until one is, guaranteeing solvability at the cost of the no-loops property.
insights.quote: If your algorithm is searching for the solution you have to be aware of the bugs and in math speak you have to look for the counter example

insights.claim: When generating puzzles constructively, it is easiest to start from a solution and add red herrings, though it is also possible to build up toward a solution.
insights.detail: Galecki's summary: every puzzle must be solvable; analytic proof or constructive generation guarantees it; and building toward a solution needs extra attention to bugs.
insights.quote: it is easiest to start off with a solution and add red herrings and trapped doors but it is possible to build up to a solution

insights.claim: Galecki sources Moondrop's puzzles from interesting maths problems, particularly graph theory, then gives them a theme that fits the cozy game, like fishing and the river grid on the damp trail.
insights.detail: Moondrop has four elemental dungeons on a mountaintop and avoids hazards like lava pits, so he looked for cozier themed puzzles.
insights.quote: Kind of looking for an interesting math problems and seeing if I can give them a theme that fits with what I am going for
